series.title: Shannon's information theory, one picture at a time
series.audience: curious beginners who know fractions but no probability theory

shorts.title: Entropy counts yes/no questions
shorts.hook: How many yes/no questions does it take, on average, to guess a letter if some letters are more likely than others?
shorts.claim: Entropy is the average number of well-chosen yes/no questions needed to identify the outcome: each outcome of probability p costs log2(1/p) questions, and H = sum of p log2(1/p).

worked_example.setup: A source sends one of four letters A, B, C, D with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 (the example in Section 10 of Shannon's paper). Ask 'Is it A?', then 'Is it B?', then 'Is it C?'.
steps: A is settled after 1 question (half the time), B after 2 (a quarter of the time), C and D after 3 (an eighth of the time each).
Writing yes as 1 and no as 0 along the path gives the code A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111; no codeword starts another, so a stream decodes uniquely.
Each letter's question count equals log2(1/p): 1, 2, 3, 3; so the average is exactly the entropy H = 1.75 bits.
Check on a typical 8-letter message AAAABBCD: 4x1 + 2x2 + 3 + 3 = 14 bits, versus 16 bits for asking 'first half or second half?' twice for every letter.
worked_example.result: H = 1.75 bits per letter: 7/4 questions on average, beating the 2 questions of the fixed halving strategy; with four equally likely letters the entropy would be exactly 2 bits.

shorts.visual: A question tree on the left: root 'A?' splits to leaf A (big block, half the width of a probability bar) and node 'B?', which splits to leaf B and node 'C?' with leaves C and D. On the right, a probability bar of four coloured blocks (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8) whose blocks slide under their leaves; each leaf's depth counter (1, 2, 3, 3) multiplies its block, and the four products stack into a running total that reaches 1.75. Then the 8-letter message turns letter by letter into its codeword bits (14 cells) beside a 16-cell fixed-length strip.
shorts.misconception: A bit is not just a 0 or 1 symbol on a wire: as a measure, it is the information in one fair yes/no answer, so an unlikely outcome carries more bits than a likely one.

practice.question: If A, B, C and D were all equally likely (1/4 each), how many yes/no questions would you need on average?
practice.answer: 2: each letter has log2(4) = 2 bits of surprise, and the best tree asks two halving questions.

shorts.reel_caption: Claude Shannon, 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' (1948): entropy is the average number of yes/no questions you need. Four letters with chances 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 need only 1.75 on average. #informationtheory #entropy #shannon
